items.title: CBT works for depression — with caveats
items.claim: Cuijpers and colleagues' meta-analyses of CBT for depression report effect sizes in the moderate range. What's the most important methodological caveat?

options.text: Most trials have substantial risk of bias (publication bias, lack of blinding, allegiance effects when researchers favour the treatment); effect sizes may be inflated by 20-50%
CBT only works for healthy people

items.reveal:
Pim Cuijpers's group has published numerous meta-analyses (Cuijpers et al. 2010, 2014, 2019). They consistently find CBT and other structured psychotherapies effective for depression but with methodological caveats: many trials are not blinded (impossible for psychotherapy), researcher allegiance correlates with effect size, publication bias remains an issue.

The NHS's IAPT (Improving Access to Psychological Therapies, 2008) made CBT widely available; routine outcomes data show recovery rates around 50% within treatment, lower than RCTs.
items.why: Treatment efficacy is layered: works in trials, sometimes less well in routine practice. The research-practice gap matters for service planning.

items.title: Chronic stress activates the HPA axis
items.claim: The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis produces cortisol in response to stress. What does chronic activation cause?

options.text: Sustained elevation of cortisol is associated with immune suppression, abdominal fat deposition, hippocampal atrophy, and increased cardiovascular risk — moving stress from a psychological to a physiological problem
Cortisol stops being produced under chronic stress

items.reveal:
Hans Selye described the General Adaptation Syndrome (alarm, resistance, exhaustion) in 1936. Bruce McEwen's concept of 'allostatic load' (1998) extends this: the wear-and-tear of repeated stress responses contributes to chronic disease.

Whitehall studies (Marmot, 1967 onwards) linked low job control with worse health outcomes via stress pathways. The relationship between psychosocial stress and cardiovascular disease is robust across cohorts but causality is hard to isolate from confounders.
items.why: The mind-body distinction breaks down when looking at chronic stress. Psychological experience produces measurable biological change with health consequences.

items.title: Deinstitutionalisation reduced asylum populations dramatically
items.claim: Following Italy's Basaglia Law (1978), the UK's Care in the Community policy (1980s-90s) and similar reforms elsewhere, what happened to inpatient psychiatric populations?

options.text: Inpatient populations fell by 60-90% in most Western countries by 2000. Outcomes were mixed: better integration for many, but inadequate community resources left some patients homeless or in the criminal justice system
Inpatient care was completely eliminated everywhere

items.reveal:
UK psychiatric inpatient beds: ~150,000 in 1955, ~22,000 by 2010. The shift was driven by both ideology (asylum critique, e.g. Goffman 'Asylums' 1961) and pharmacology (chlorpromazine, 1952).

Where community resources followed (Trieste, Italy under Basaglia), outcomes were generally positive. Where they didn't (UK and US in different ways), gaps in care emerged — over-representation of severely mentally ill people in prisons and homelessness is widely documented.
items.why: Major mental health policy changes have decades-long consequences. The reduction in coercive asylum care was widely accepted; the under-investment in community alternatives is the unresolved part.
